title: Ask What It Looks Like Before You Defend Yourself
author: Is Public Speaking
summary: The newsletter Is Public Speaking argues that the instinctive reaction to a vague complaint, 'I wish you showed you cared more,' is to defend against a definition you invented yourself rather than the one the other person actually means, which ends the conversation without resolving the feeling. The piece offers a three-question sequence, what does it look like, what kind, how does it feel when it's missing, that works identically in a marriage argument at 9pm or a workplace meeting at 9:15am, arguing that a calm clarifying question lowers the emotional temperature and usually reveals a smaller, more specific request than the one you braced to argue about.
points: Diagnoses a common conversational failure: responding to your own definition of a vague complaint instead of asking what the other person actually means.
Provides a transferable three-question sequence, what does it look like, what kind, how does it feel when missing, for both personal and professional contexts.
Argues a clarifying question lowers emotional temperature and invites future honesty, while a rebuttal, even an accurate one, punishes disclosure.
Notes most 'abstract' requests turn out to be smaller and more specific than the version a defensive listener braced to argue about.
quotes: Somebody tells you what they need from you, and within four seconds you are explaining why they already have it.
What you did was answer a complaint you had not understood yet. "Show me you care" means something specific in their head, and you responded to your own version of it rather than theirs.

The cost lands twice: in the moment, they learn that raising something gets them a rebuttal, so next time they say nothing. Over a longer stretch, the unraised things accumulate, and resentment is mostly a pile of conversations that got argued with instead of understood.

A calm, neutral question tells the other person the conversation is survivable. People say the real thing only when the first thing did not get punished, and a rebuttal is a punishment even when it is accurate.

Ask how it feels when it is missing: this is the one people skip and it does the most work. "How do you feel when that is not there?" The answer, disconnected or lonely or unseen, is the thing you are actually being asked to address.
